newsitem.title: INDIA: METALS - Aluminium demand, supply match by 2002.
newsitem.headline: METALS - Aluminium demand, supply match by 2002.

text.p: India's aluminium production is expected to match demand by 2002 with new capacities coming on stream but the country will face a shortfall in the intervening years, industry officials said on Monday.
S.N. Johri, chairman of state-run National Aluminium Company (NALCO), said aluminium demand was expected to grow at eight percent annually for the next five years.
"By the turn of the century the demand is likely to touch 800,000 tonnes, against a production of approximately 580,000 tonnes," Johri told Reuters.
Johri said with no greenfield projects starting production so far no metal will come from new plants till 2001.
He said a substantial increase in output was expected only in 2002 when smelter and refinery capacity expansions currently planned by some producers become operational.
"The gap has to be met by imports until such time," Johri said. India currently allows free imports and exports of aluminium.
The country produced 523,849 tonnes of aluminium in 1996/97 (April-March), slightly up from 521,031 tonnes in the previous year.

India has four major aluminium firms, Hindalco and Indian Aluminium Company Ltd (INDAL), both in the private sector, and state-run NALCO and Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. The country has an annual installed capacity of 670,000 tonnes of aluminium.
Johri said that as demand would outstrip production for the next few years, India would have to cut its aluminium exports.
"It is imperative (with the surging aluminium demand), there will be some reduction in the exports of the aluminium metal from India," Johri said.
NALCO, Asia's largest aluminium maker, is a major exporter. It exported 65,000 tonnes of the metal in 1996/97.

Johri said that NALCO had sent a proposal to the governmemnt to expand its smelter capacity to 345,000 tonnes annually from the current 220,000 tonnes and an increase in power generation capacity to 960 megawatt from 760.
"The necessary clearances from the government are expected shortly," Johri said.

He said other plans by NALCO include expanding its bauxite mines capacity to 4.8 million tonnes annually from 2.4 million and alumina refinery capacity to 1.58 million tonnes from the current 800,000 tonnes.
"The work on these areas of expansion is in progress and is likely to be completed within four years' time," Johri said.
"With this expansion and the expansion envisaged by other primary producers, India can look for some relief in its metal requirement in 2002," he said.
"We expect a metal shortage in the domestic aluminium industry around 1998/99, mainly due to capacity constraints," said a senior INDAL official.
The official told Reuters that the firm had tied up with Norway's Norsk Hydro ASA to set up a one-million-tonne alumina refinery in eastern Orissa state.
"The 40 billion rupee ($1.12 billion) joint venture is progressing on schedule," the INDAL official said. "The land acquisition process for the project is almost complete."
INDAL produced 39,839 tonnes of aluminium in 1996/97, down from 58,694 tonnes in the previous year.

Johri said foreign firms like Switzerland's Alusuisse-Lonza Group and South Africa's Gencor Ltd have shown keen interest in setting up smelters in India and manufacturing and marketing value-added aluminium products.
($1 = 35.8 rupees)
